Her symptoms began at age 8 years

She had previously tried multiple medications including systemic steroids, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, tofacitinib, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), with minimal improvement
Violaceous erythema on forehead and midface
Diffuse poikiloderma involving upper chest, anterolateral thighs, and extensor arms
Erythematous, flat-topped papules on extensor joints of hands
Nailfold examination showed dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles
Elevated serum IFN-β levels (8 pg/mL, normal ≤2 pg/mL)
Presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies
Radiographic evidence of myositis
Confirmatory skin biopsy performed

The patient's history of trying multiple medications with minimal improvement, along with the presence of autoantibodies and elevated serum IFN-β levels, suggests an underlying autoimmune disorder.

The confirmatory skin biopsy performed explains the diagnosis of Amyopathic Dermatomyositis, a subtype of dermatomyositis.

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of progressive, multiple itchy erythematous to violaceous papules and plaques, along with histopathologic examination revealing dermoepidermal separation and milia, is consistent with Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa, a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the COL7A1 gene, as confirmed by whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing.

The patient's presentation of pruritic erythematous to violaceous lichenified papules and plaques on the left shin is consistent with Lichenified Dermatitis, a dermatological condition characterized by chronic itching and scratching, leading to lichenification of the skin.

The patient's histopathologic examination revealing dermoepidermal separation is also consistent with Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita, an inflammatory condition characterized by autoantibodies against type VII collagen, although the genetic variant in COL7A1 suggests a dystrophic form.

The patient's presentation of multiple milia, both clinically and histopathologically, suggests a milia-associated disorder, although this is not a specific diagnosable disease entity, it is a characteristic feature of several dermatological conditions.

rationales.F01: The presence of progressive, multiple itchy erythematous to violaceous papules and plaques localized to the left shin for more than 10 years is suggestive of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa.
rationales.F02: The presence of milia and a few erosions with partially detached epidermis is consistent with both Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa and Milia-associated Disorder.
rationales.F07: The histopathologic examination revealing dermoepidermal separation is highly suggestive of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa and rules out Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita.
rationales.F09: The identification of a novel heterozygous missense variant in COL7A1 is highly suggestive of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa and rules out Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita.
rationales.F10: The confirmation of cosegregation of the variant by Sanger sequencing further supports the diagnosis of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa.
